nuggets.title: Metric flap triggers evaluator storm and dropped pages

scenario.symptoms: During a deploy, CPU metric flapped every 30 s causing 12,000 alert evaluations per minute. PagerDuty throttled and real outages went unpageable.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Evaluator reruns on every raw sample with no hysteresis or grouping window; state store writes synchronously on each flap.

incident.headline: No hysteresis causes alert state thrashing

agenda.goal: Design an evaluation engine that supports both time-based and event-based triggers.
agenda.opener: Alerts stopped firing when metrics flapped—the evaluator loop is highlighted. What failed?

evidence.strong: Uses a hybrid approach: a scheduler for time-based rules and an event bus listening to pipeline completions for event-driven checks.
evidence.adequate: Relies purely on a scheduler like Airflow or a cron service polling every few minutes.
evidence.weak: Attempts to evaluate all rules sequentially in a single process.

misconceptions.pattern: Only uses cron to poll the warehouse constantly.
misconceptions.challenge: If a pipeline finishes at 2:03 AM, how quickly does the cron job catch it without wasting warehouse compute by polling every minute?

probes: How do we prevent overloading the data warehouse if thousands of rules run at exactly midnight?
Can we trigger a check immediately when an ETL job finishes?
hints: Think about how an orchestrator might notify our system.
Could we use an event queue to decouple the trigger from the execution worker?
agenda.referenceFix: For-duration conditions, grouping windows, alert suppression during known deploys, rate-limit pages, and async state updates with debouncing.

nuggets.title: Same incident pages on-call twenty times

scenario.symptoms: Database failover generated 22 identical PagerDuty incidents because each shard evaluator opened a new alert key instead of deduping on correlation id.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Alert fingerprint excludes service and shard labels; dedupe TTL too short for long incidents.

agenda.goal: Maintain an alert state machine to prevent noisy duplicate alerts for ongoing issues.
agenda.opener: One DB incident woke everyone repeatedly—the dedupe path is highlighted. How do you correlate?

evidence.strong: Introduces a state store (like Redis or Postgres) to track alert status (OK, Firing, Resolved) and only notifies on state transitions or escalation intervals.
evidence.adequate: Silences the specific rule ID for a hardcoded time window using a cache.
evidence.weak: Relies entirely on the downstream tool (like PagerDuty) to handle deduplication.

misconceptions.pattern: Fires a notification every time the check returns false.
misconceptions.challenge: Won't this create an alert storm and page the on-call engineer every 5 minutes for the same issue?

probes: Where exactly are you storing the fact that this alert is already active?
How does the system know when to send a 'Resolved' notification?
hints: We need to remember what happened in the previous run.
Think about using a key-value store to track the current state of each rule.
agenda.referenceFix: Stable alert fingerprint on root cause labels, correlation ids from traces, merge windows, and inhibit rules linking shard alerts to parent.

nuggets.title: On-call drowned in per-shard CPU alerts

scenario.symptoms: Night shift received 400 CPU alerts from individual Kafka brokers though cluster capacity was fine. Mean time to acknowledge rose above 30 minutes.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Rules fire per broker without roll-up; no top-N or cluster-level aggregation.

incident.headline: Missing roll-up groups shard noise into fatigue

agenda.goal: Group related alerts by upstream root causes to prevent alert storms.
agenda.opener: Brokers spammed pages but the cluster was healthy—the grouping path is highlighted. How do you roll up?

evidence.strong: Uses data lineage to identify the upstream root cause, suppresses downstream alerts, and sends one grouped notification detailing the blast radius.
evidence.adequate: Batches alerts by team and time window, sending a single digest message.
evidence.weak: Suggests aggressive global rate limiting, dropping notifications entirely.

misconceptions.pattern: Just rate limit the team to 5 alerts per hour.
misconceptions.challenge: If we drop alerts, how will the team know about the other 35 datasets that are currently broken once the first issue is fixed?

probes: How can the system programmatically know that these 40 tables depend on the same upstream table?
If we delay sending to group them, how long do we wait?
hints: Consider grouping alerts that happen in the same time window.
Does your metadata catalog track dependencies between tables?
agenda.referenceFix: Multi-level rules with cluster roll-up, inhibition when parent fires, dynamic top-N offenders, and on-call policies requiring grouped incidents.

nuggets.title: Deploy broke alert rule without anyone noticing

scenario.symptoms: A typo in label matcher stopped all payment error alerts for six days until finance noticed reconciliation gaps. CI had no alert rule tests.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Rules edited via UI without version control; staging environment lacks representative metrics for dry-run.

incident.headline: Untested rule change silenced critical alerts

agenda.goal: Provide a safe mechanism for teams to test new rules without causing false alarms.
agenda.opener: Payment alerts silently stopped—the rule testing path is highlighted. How do you catch regressions?

evidence.strong: Proposes a shadow mode or dry-run evaluation that logs rule outcomes without triggering the notification pipeline.
evidence.adequate: Suggests running rules against a staging environment or routing to a private test channel.
evidence.weak: Assumes users will just test SQL queries manually before deploying.

probes: Can we backtest a new rule against the last 7 days of data?
hints: What if the rule evaluates normally but skips the final sending step?
Could we add a 'status' field to the rule definition like 'testing' or 'active'?
agenda.referenceFix: Git-backed rules, unit tests with fixture time series, staging dry-run on replayed data, canary notifications, and synthetic alert probes.

nuggets.title: Friday traffic spike pages false anomaly

scenario.symptoms: Every Friday evening on-call gets paged for 'anomaly' on signups though pattern is normal weekly seasonality. Trust in anomaly alerts eroded.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Anomaly detector uses fixed z-score without day-of-week baseline; training window too short.

agenda.goal: Support dynamic baselines and seasonality for metric evaluation.
agenda.opener: Predictable Friday spikes page people—the anomaly model path is highlighted. How do you fix signal?

evidence.strong: Stores historical metric aggregates in a time-series DB and calculates z-scores or uses trailing windows with seasonality awareness to define the baseline.
evidence.adequate: Compares the current value to a simple 7-day moving average.
evidence.weak: Suggests adding 'weekend' hardcoded rules to every configuration.

probes: Where are we storing the historical data needed to calculate this baseline?
How do we prevent a baseline from skewing if the data has been broken for 3 days?
hints: We need to compare today's value with previous days.
Think about storing historical check results in a fast timeseries database.
agenda.referenceFix: Seasonal baselines by hour and weekday, robust statistics, alert only on residual after deseasoning, and feedback loop to tune sensitivity.
